# Chemical elements and conservation of mass (`chemical_elements`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: helped by oxygen_combustion, pneumatic_chemistry_gases, measurement_quantification
- Core idea: Earth, water, air and fire are not elements. An element is a substance that no chemical operation can split further: gold, iron, copper, lead, tin, mercury, sulphur, carbon, and the gases oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen. Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen; air is a mixture. In every reaction the total weight of what goes in equals the total weight of what comes out, provided the gases are caught and weighed too, so the balance is the chemist's main instrument. Elements do not turn into one another, which is why base metals cannot be made into gold.
- Pitfalls:
  - Listing as elements things that are compounds or mixtures (water, air, salt, lime, steel, bronze).
  - Forgetting the gases when weighing, which seems to disprove conservation.
  - Mocking alchemists as fools. Their apparatus and many of their substances are real and useful; only transmutation fails.
  - Calling heat and light elements, as Lavoisier's own list still did.
- History: greece: 5th–4th c. BC – four elements of Empedocles and Aristotle, the theory to be replaced; china: from c. 4th c. BC – five phases (wuxing); a scheme of processes rather than of substances; india: from c. 6th c. BC – five great elements (mahabhuta) in several schools; islamic: 8th–10th c. – sulphur-mercury theory of metals in the Jabirian corpus; c. 1025 Ibn Sina argues against transmutation; europe: 1661 – Boyle criticises the old elements; 1756 Lomonosov and 1770s Lavoisier establish conservation of weight; 1789 Lavoisier's list of 33 simple substances
- Read:
  - Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier, Traité élémentaire de chimie (1789)
  - Robert Boyle, The Sceptical Chymist (1661)
  - William H. Brock, The Fontana History of Chemistry (1992)
